Retrieval returns similar prior chest X-rays for education and reference.
Prior work studies embeddings and scarce or imbalanced categories.
Balanced index-size experiments preserve the target class proportion.
This study fixes gallery size and reduces target prevalence from 5% to 0.5%.

Denner et al. [1] varied the number of indexed examples per class in a balanced index, changing absolute support while preserving prevalence. Rare and imbalanced settings also appear in SISH [2] and volumetric retrieval [4]. The present narrative review identified a gap in controlled multi-level prevalence reductions with queries and representations held fixed. The comparison with prior work is conceptual, not a numerical cross-study benchmark.
Source: supplied Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx. Reference numbers follow the manuscript.
Measure retrieval loss as target prevalence falls across three target pathologies.
Compare six ResNet-50 conditions using fixed queries, checkpoints and gallery size.
Show why retrieval benchmarks should report more than one gallery prevalence.

Primary question: how does target-prevalence decline affect retrieval across models and pathologies? Secondary question: from the same SwAV initialization, how does supervised contrastive adaptation compare with classification? The study is an evaluation protocol, not a newly proposed backbone architecture.
Source: supplied Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx. Reference numbers follow the manuscript.
Data: NIH, SIIM-ACR and three external chest X-ray collections
Models: six pretrained or adapted ResNet-50 conditions
Protocol: 200 queries per target, 20,000 images per gallery
Prevalence: 5%, 2%, 1% and 0.5%, with five gallery samples each
Embedding extraction and exact retrieval workflow

Three evaluated targets: cardiomegaly, emphysema and pneumothorax. Relevant target counts are 1,000, 400, 200 or 100 per 20,000-image gallery. Three non-target pathology distractors contribute 400 images each. Background fills the remaining gallery positions. There are 60 galleries in total. NIH target-positive patients are excluded from adaptation/background partitions. NIH adaptation uses 48,280 training and 12,266 validation images. Common-class adaptation uses 4,545 source-class-balanced images split 80:20. Query patients are excluded where identifiers permit. TB was excluded as an evaluated target after a source-bias audit, but remains a fixed 2% distractor. The pipeline describes an exact exhaustive search using normalized embeddings.

CNN-PT: supervised ImageNet ResNet-50 without adaptation. CNN-Common: normal/pneumonia/COVID-19 classification. CNN-NIH: NIH multi-label classification. SwAV-PT: ImageNet self-supervised SwAV without adaptation. SwAV-CLS: the same NIH classification objective as CNN-NIH, from SwAV. SwAV-SupCon: weighted multi-label supervised contrastive adaptation from SwAV. All provide 2,048-D backbone embeddings. SupCon uses two views of 64 source images, label-set Jaccard weights, temperature 0.07 and a training-only projection head. AdamW learning rate and weight decay are 0.0001, with up to 50 epochs and early stopping. Checkpoint selection uses objective-specific validation losses. Five gallery seeds measure gallery resampling, not independent retraining. Available fine-tuning annotations exclude target labels, but this does not verify clinical absence of targets in every image.
Source: supplied Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx. Reference numbers follow the manuscript.
SwAV-SupCon leads at every pathology–prevalence setting.
It exceeds SwAV-CLS in 10 of 12 globally corrected comparisons.

The chart shows an unweighted arithmetic mean of the three pathology means at 0.5% target prevalence for four selected conditions, calculated from manuscript Table 2. Values: CNN-PT 0.0210; SwAV-PT 0.0275667; SwAV-CLS 0.0251333; SwAV-SupCon 0.0386. The display rounds to four decimals. CNN-Common and CNN-NIH were also evaluated, as listed in the setup table. The chart presents descriptive means, not a pooled inferential comparison. The claim of ten significant contrasts refers to query-paired SwAV-SupCon versus SwAV-CLS tests across all twelve pathology-prevalence conditions, globally Holm-corrected within 72 planned model comparisons. Exceptions: cardiomegaly at 0.5% and 1%. The strongest low-prevalence absolute P@10 values are 0.0163, 0.0335 and 0.0660 for cardiomegaly, emphysema and pneumothorax. Their enrichment over random expectation 0.005 is 3.26, 6.70 and 13.20 times. Pneumothorax is a cross-source condition and these means do not establish clinical utility.
Source: supplied Chest_XRay_Retrieval_IEEE_Format.docx. Reference numbers follow the manuscript.

The first displayed range rounds the manuscript relative P@10 loss range 83.4%-91.9% to whole percentages. All eighteen model-pathology endpoint contrasts show significant decline for both P@10 and nDCG@10 after Holm correction, adjusted p ≤ 2.30e-26. Absolute P@10 losses range from 0.0959 to 0.3480. SwAV-SupCon has the highest mean P@10 at all twelve pathology-prevalence conditions. Ten of its twelve planned contrasts against SwAV-CLS survive global correction. At 0.5%, adjusted p-values for SupCon versus CLS are >0.99 for cardiomegaly, 5.34e-7 for emphysema and 3.17e-6 for pneumothorax. A larger absolute loss can accompany better endpoint retrieval: on pneumothorax, SupCon loses 0.3480 versus CLS 0.2841, while remaining higher at both endpoints.

Lower prevalence reduces retrieval quality across every evaluated model.
One training run and source confounding limit the SupCon finding.
Repeat training and strengthen controls across dataset sources.
Test lower target counts and obtain clinician-assessed relevance.

Conclusions concern the evaluated ResNet-50 conditions, three targets and prevalence protocol. Single checkpoints do not estimate retraining variation. Classification and SupCon checkpoints use objective-specific selection criteria. SIIM supplies pneumothorax queries and NIH supplies relevant gallery images, aligning source with retrieval role. Labels are imperfect, and external metadata cannot establish exhaustive finding annotations. Zero-shot therefore means target labels were absent from available adaptation labels. No radiologist judged relevance or diagnostic benefit. The lowest prevalence still has 100 relevant images; much larger approximate indexes and lower absolute counts remain untested. Report at least two clinically relevant gallery-prevalence levels.
